name: Oxazepam (Serax)
summary: Short-acting benzodiazepine used for short-term anxiety relief and for symptoms of alcohol withdrawal. Slower to kick in than some benzos, but often chosen when liver function is a concern. High dependence risk—keep it short and keep it supervised.
description: Oxazepam is a benzodiazepine used for short-term anxiety relief and for alcohol withdrawal symptoms like tremor and intense anxiety. It can make you sleepy, foggy, and unsteady—especially if you combine it with alcohol, opioids, or other sedatives. Dependence can happen with ongoing use. If you’ve taken it regularly, don’t stop abruptly—taper slowly with a clinician to avoid dangerous withdrawal.
patient_summary: Oxazepam can calm anxiety and help with alcohol withdrawal symptoms, but it can also knock you out, slow your thinking, and mess with balance. Mixing it with alcohol or opioids is a hard no because it can suppress breathing. If you take it daily for a while, your body can get dependent—so stopping needs a taper, not a cold turkey.

linked_conditions.context: Used for short-term relief of severe anxiety symptoms, often as a bridge while first-line treatments (therapy and SSRIs/SNRIs) take effect.
Used to manage alcohol withdrawal symptoms like tremor and anxiety. It’s sometimes preferred when liver function is impaired because it’s metabolized mainly via glucuronidation.

Not a first-choice sleep medication, but sedation can indirectly help sleep during acute anxiety or withdrawal. Long-term use for sleep is generally a bad tradeoff because of tolerance and dependence.
May be used short-term for anxiety-driven agitation, but it is not an antidepressant or antipsychotic and is not indicated for psychosis.

contraindications: Hypersensitivity to oxazepam or any component of the formulation
Canadian labeling (not in all US labeling): history of glaucoma, myasthenia gravis, use in infants

efficacy_response.metric: Symptom relief in acute anxiety / withdrawal
efficacy_response.patient_text: Oxazepam can reduce the physical intensity of anxiety and withdrawal symptoms, but response varies a lot person-to-person. The bigger clinical story is less about a single trial number and more about using the lowest effective dose for the shortest time to avoid dependence.

pharmacokinetics.absorption: Slowly absorbed from the GI tract
pharmacokinetics.half_life: ~8 hours (range: 6-11 hours; can be longer in very old age or severe renal impairment)
pharmacokinetics.duration_IR: Classified as short-acting; effects often last several hours
pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Hepatic glucuronidation (phase II) to an inactive metabolite

sections.heading: What It's Used For
sections.text: Oxazepam is a short-acting benzodiazepine used for short-term anxiety relief and for managing symptoms of alcohol withdrawal (like tremor and intense anxiety). In psychiatry, it’s usually a “get you through the storm” medication—not a long-term daily solution.
items: {link:condition:generalized-anxiety-disorder:Anxiety disorders}: Short-term relief when symptoms are severe or disabling
{link:condition:alcohol-withdrawal:Alcohol withdrawal syndrome}: Reduces withdrawal symptoms like tremor, anxiety, and agitation
Bridge strategy: Temporary symptom control while first-line anxiety treatment (therapy and SSRIs/SNRIs) ramps up
off_label: Sleep disruption during acute anxiety or withdrawal (not preferred long-term)

sections.heading: What People Feel
sections.intro: Everyone’s nervous system is different, but these are the patterns I see again and again:

quotes: It didn’t hit me like a lightning bolt—more like a slow exhale.
I noticed my body unclenched before my mind did.
The panic didn’t vanish, but it got quieter and more manageable.
I felt calmer… and also kind of wiped out.
It’s like my thoughts were wrapped in cotton.
Helpful at night, annoying during the day.
items.note: Sleepiness and cognitive slowing are dose-dependent and worse with other sedatives.

quotes: I was a little wobbly on my feet.
Going down stairs felt weirdly risky.
I could tell my reaction time was slower.
items.note: This is a bigger deal in older adults, especially if there’s already fall risk.

quotes: After a while, the same dose didn’t feel like it did at first.
I didn’t think I was dependent until I tried to stop.
Missing a dose made my anxiety rebound hard.
items.note: Physical dependence risk increases with higher doses and longer duration.

quotes: Instead of calming me down, it made me edgy and agitated.
I felt weirdly impulsive and not like myself.
It was supposed to sedate me, but I got revved up.
items.note: If a benzo makes you more aggressive, wired, or out of control, that’s a red flag—contact your prescriber quickly.

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: Oxazepam is considered short-acting, but it’s not always the fastest benzo to feel. It tends to come on more gradually, which some people prefer (less “hit”) and others hate (less immediate relief).
key_points: About 1-2 hours: Many people start feeling calmer (varies)
~3 hours: Peak blood levels (strongest effects often live around here)
Short-acting classification: Effects usually fade over the same day, but sedation can linger if you’re sensitive or combining sedatives

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.text: Oxazepam can be effective for short-term anxiety relief and for alcohol withdrawal symptoms, especially when dosing is tailored to symptom severity. The key is using it in the right situation: acute, time-limited, and monitored—because the downside risk (dependence, sedation, interactions) rises fast when it becomes routine.
sections.clinical_details: For alcohol withdrawal, benzodiazepines are commonly used either symptom-triggered (based on a validated scale like CIWA-Ar) or fixed-dose regimens depending on setting and seizure/DT risk. Oxazepam is sometimes chosen when hepatic concerns make certain longer-acting options less attractive. For anxiety disorders, it’s generally positioned as short-term relief while first-line treatments take effect.

citation.title: Oxazepam prescribing information; ASAM Alcohol Withdrawal Management Guideline

sections.heading: Critical Safety Information
sections.highlight: Mixing benzodiazepines with opioids or alcohol can shut down breathing. This can be fatal.
sections.black_box: Concomitant use of benzodiazepines and opioids may result in profound sedation, respiratory depression, coma, and death. Reserve combined prescribing for patients with inadequate alternative options. Limit dosages and durations to the minimum required and monitor for respiratory depression and sedation.
other: Abuse, misuse, and addiction risk: higher with alcohol, other sedatives, or illicit substances
Physical dependence can develop with continued use; risk rises with dose and duration
Abrupt stopping after continued use can cause severe, potentially life-threatening withdrawal
CNS depression: impaired driving, judgment, reaction time
Respiratory disease (COPD, sleep apnea): higher risk of dangerous sedation and breathing suppression
Depression and suicidality: avoid in depression when possible due to risk of worsening mood symptoms (except acute/emergency situations)
patient_counseling: No alcohol. Not “just one drink.” This combo is where people get hurt.
Avoid opioids if at all possible. If there’s no alternative, keep doses and duration minimal and monitor closely.
Don’t drive or operate machinery until you know exactly how you respond.
If you’ve been taking it regularly, do not stop suddenly—ask for a taper plan.
Tell your prescriber if you have a history of substance use, overdose, or medication misuse.
Get help urgently if you have extreme sleepiness, slow/shallow breathing, blue lips, or you can’t stay awake.

sections.heading: Side Effects
sections.summary: Most common: sleepiness, dizziness, slowed thinking, and unsteady coordination. Most dangerous: respiratory depression (especially with opioids/alcohol) and severe withdrawal if stopped abruptly after regular use.
plain_language_list: Memory issues (especially forming new memories while it’s active)

common.patient_note: Expect some sedation, especially early on or after dose increases. If you feel over-sedated, that’s not a “push through it” situation—dose often needs adjusting.
Can feel like lightheadedness or being slightly off-balance. Hydration, slow position changes, and avoiding other sedatives help—but sometimes the dose is simply too high.
This is the fall-risk side effect. If you’re older, already unsteady, or on other sedating meds, this matters a lot.
Benzos can interfere with forming new memories while they’re active. If you don’t remember conversations or decisions, that’s a sign to reassess the plan.
Often a marker of being too sedated—especially if paired with unsteady walking.
Rare but important. If you get more wired, impulsive, angry, or aggressive on a benzo, stop and call your prescriber—this can escalate.

serious: Respiratory depression, coma, and death—risk skyrockets with opioids, alcohol, and other sedatives
Severe withdrawal reactions with abrupt discontinuation after continued use (can be life-threatening)
Syncope or severe hypotension (rare but possible), especially in people who can’t tolerate BP drops
Hazardous sleep-related behaviors (sleep-driving, cooking/eating while asleep) with amnesia
Worsening depression or suicidality in vulnerable patients

sections.heading: Critical Drug Interactions
sections.intro: Oxazepam can stack sedation with almost anything that slows the nervous system. The big danger isn’t subtle—it’s breathing suppression and loss of consciousness.

items.with: Opioids (prescription pain meds, illicit opioids, fentanyl exposure)
items.risk: Profound sedation, respiratory depression, coma, death (boxed warning class effect).
items.action: Avoid if possible. If there is no alternative: minimum effective doses, shortest duration, and close monitoring for sedation and breathing problems.

items.risk: Additive/synergistic CNS and respiratory depression; blackouts, falls, overdose risk.
items.action: Do not combine. If alcohol use is part of the picture, prescribers need a plan that prioritizes safety.

items.with: Other sedatives (sleep meds, sedating antihistamines, muscle relaxants, some antipsychotics)
items.risk: Extra sedation, confusion, falls, impaired driving, breathing suppression in high-risk patients.
items.action: Use extreme caution. Consider dose reductions, timing changes, or alternative meds.

items.risk: More sedation, slowed reaction time, increased accident risk, worse cognition.
items.action: Avoid combining, especially if you’re driving or operating machinery.

items.with: Medications that lower blood pressure or cause dizziness
items.action: Stand slowly, monitor symptoms, and reassess the regimen if you’re wobbling or fainting.

sections.heading: Safe Discontinuation
sections.text: If oxazepam has been used regularly, stopping suddenly can trigger a withdrawal syndrome that ranges from miserable to medically dangerous. The safer move is a gradual taper that slows down if symptoms flare.
key_points: Dependence risk increases with higher daily doses and longer treatment duration.
Abrupt discontinuation or rapid dose reduction after continued use can precipitate acute withdrawal reactions that may be life-threatening.
Typical low-to-moderate dose taper (no major benzo use disorder concern): reduce the total daily dose by ~20-25% every week based on response and tolerability.
Extended/high-dose therapy or suspected benzodiazepine use disorder: reduce total daily dose by ~25% every 1-2 weeks, often faster early and slower later as the taper progresses.
Because oxazepam is shorter-acting, some clinicians consider switching to an equivalent dose of a longer-acting benzodiazepine to smooth the taper in select cases.
Goal: detect re-emerging symptoms, reduce rebound anxiety/insomnia, and avoid severe withdrawal.

sections.heading: Dosing Information
sections.text: Oxazepam dosing depends on what you’re treating: anxiety dosing is scheduled and titrated; alcohol withdrawal dosing is often protocol-based (symptom-triggered or fixed-dose). Exact dosing should match the setting (inpatient vs outpatient), symptom severity, and safety risks (especially opioids, respiratory disease, older age, and substance use history).

adult.anxiety_titration: Increase total daily dose in increments of 15-30 mg every 2-3 days based on response and tolerability
adult.alcohol_withdrawal_symptom_triggered_prn: 15-30 mg PO as needed per institution-specific protocol until appropriate sedation achieved; dose/frequency guided by a validated scale such as CIWA-Ar
adult.alcohol_withdrawal_breakthrough_prn: Up to 5 additional PRN doses of 15-30 mg PO over a 4-day treatment period for breakthrough symptoms (hold for excessive sedation)
adult.safety_note: Reduce dose or avoid use with opioids or significant chronic disease (especially respiratory compromise). Avoid use in patients with a history of substance use, medication misuse, or depression unless there’s a clear short-term rationale and close monitoring.

sections.simple_explanation: For anxiety, oxazepam is usually taken in divided doses and adjusted slowly. For alcohol withdrawal, dosing is often guided by symptoms (like a CIWA-Ar score) or a fixed taper schedule, with extra doses only if symptoms break through—while watching closely for oversedation.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, Special Groups
sections.text: Benzodiazepines in pregnancy and breastfeeding require careful risk-benefit thinking. In alcohol withdrawal during pregnancy, treatment shouldn’t be delayed when symptoms are serious—but inpatient monitoring is typically recommended. In older adults, benzodiazepines increase risk of confusion, falls, and accidents, so they’re generally avoided unless there’s a strong reason.
sections.pregnancy: Oxazepam crosses the placenta. Benzodiazepine exposure late in pregnancy may cause neonatal sedation (hypotonia, lethargy, respiratory depression) and/or neonatal withdrawal symptoms (irritability, tremors, feeding difficulties). Data on birth-defect risk are mixed and not perfectly conclusive, so this becomes a shared decision: severity of illness, alternatives, and timing in pregnancy matter. For alcohol withdrawal in pregnancy, benzodiazepines are commonly used and inpatient treatment is generally recommended; near delivery, agents with shorter onset/duration may be preferred and newborn monitoring is important.
sections.lactation: Oxazepam is present in breast milk. Case reports describe measurable milk concentrations, and infant sedation has been reported with benzodiazepines as a class in some cases. If oxazepam is used while breastfeeding, use the lowest effective dose and monitor the infant for excessive sleepiness, poor feeding, breathing problems, and poor weight gain. Some guidance considers shorter half-life benzodiazepines more reasonable than long half-life agents with active metabolites when a benzo is necessary.
sections.pediatrics: Children >12 years and adolescents: refer to adult dosing. Routine psychiatric use in younger patients is generally avoided due to safety risks and paradoxical reactions.
sections.geriatrics: Beers Criteria flags benzodiazepines as potentially inappropriate in adults ≥65 because of increased risk of cognitive impairment, delirium, falls, fractures, and motor vehicle crashes. If a benzodiazepine is truly necessary (for example, severe anxiety or alcohol withdrawal), use the lowest dose, reassess frequently, and taper as soon as clinically reasonable. Suggested anxiety dosing in older adults: start 10 mg PO three times daily; if needed, increase cautiously to 15 mg PO 3-4 times daily.
sections.hepatic: No specific manufacturer dose adjustment is provided, and hepatic dysfunction is not expected to significantly decrease clearance. Clinically, oxazepam is often considered when hepatic concerns exist because metabolism is primarily glucuronidation. Still: start low, go slow, and watch sedation.
sections.renal: No manufacturer dose adjustment provided; adjustment is unlikely based on available evidence, though half-life may be prolonged in severe renal insufficiency. Hemodialysis: not dialyzable (minimal removal).

sections.heading: Clinical Monitoring
items: Respiratory status: especially if COPD, sleep apnea, obesity hypoventilation, or any opioid exposure (monitor for slow/shallow breathing and excessive sedation).
Sedation and psychomotor impairment: falls risk, driving risk, reaction time; reassess after dose changes.
Misuse/addiction risk: early refills, dose escalation, lost prescriptions, using with alcohol/illicit substances, multiple prescribers/pharmacies.
Mood changes: worsening depression, emotional blunting, irritability, suicidal thoughts—especially in vulnerable patients.
Paradoxical reactions: agitation, aggression, impulsivity—stop/reassess if this shows up.
Withdrawal risk: if doses are missed or reduced; slow the taper if rebound symptoms are intense.
Periodic labs (as clinically indicated): CBC and liver function tests.
Cardiovascular monitoring when relevant: hypotension, syncope risk in medically fragile patients.

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: Oxazepam is available as oral capsules or tablets depending on country. The practical dosing reality is that the available strengths shape taper steps.
items: US (oral capsules, generic): 10 mg, 15 mg, 30 mg
Canada (oral tablets, generic): 10 mg, 15 mg, 30 mg

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: Oxazepam enhances the effect of GABA, the brain’s main calming signal. Think of GABA like a brake pedal for overactive threat circuits. When oxazepam boosts GABA signaling at GABA-A receptors, neurons become less excitable, which can reduce anxiety, agitation, and withdrawal symptoms—but also causes sedation, slowed thinking, and coordination problems.

sections.heading: Place in Treatment Algorithm
sections.text: Oxazepam has a clear niche: short-term symptom control for severe anxiety or alcohol withdrawal. For chronic anxiety disorders, it’s usually not the long-game—therapy and SSRIs/SNRIs are the foundation. In alcohol withdrawal, it may be used as part of symptom-triggered or fixed-dose protocols, especially when clinicians want a benzodiazepine option that’s often considered friendlier in hepatic impairment. The core principle stays the same: lowest effective dose, shortest necessary duration, and a real taper plan if use becomes regular.

seo.title: Oxazepam (Serax): Uses, Dosage, Side Effects, Interactions & Tapering
seo.description: Oxazepam (Serax) for short-term anxiety relief and alcohol withdrawal symptoms: dosing regimens, side effects (sedation, falls), dangerous interactions with opioids/alcohol, and how to taper safely.

editorial.reviewStatement: Content medically reviewed and verified against FDA prescribing information, APA clinical practice guidelines, and current peer-reviewed literature.

faqs.a: Oxazepam is used for short-term treatment of anxiety disorders and for managing symptoms of alcohol withdrawal (like tremor, anxiety, and agitation). In practice, it’s usually a short-term stabilizer—not a long-term daily anxiety plan.

Oxazepam tends to come on more gradually than some other benzodiazepines. Many people feel effects within about 1-2 hours, and peak levels are around 3 hours. If you need instant rescue relief, oxazepam may feel slower.

It’s classified as a short-acting benzodiazepine with an average half-life around 8 hours (often quoted range 6-11 hours). Effects can last several hours, and sedation can linger longer if you’re sensitive or taking other sedating medications.

faqs.q: Can I take oxazepam with opioids?
faqs.a: This combination is high risk. Benzodiazepines plus opioids can cause profound sedation, respiratory depression, coma, and death. If a clinician decides there’s truly no alternative, the safest approach is minimum effective doses, minimum duration, and close monitoring for oversedation and breathing problems.

faqs.q: Can I drink alcohol while taking oxazepam?
faqs.a: No. Alcohol and oxazepam is a dangerous combo—sedation and breathing suppression can stack and turn into an emergency. If alcohol use is part of the picture, your prescriber should know so the plan can be built around safety.

It can be. Like other benzodiazepines, oxazepam carries risk of misuse and addiction, and physical dependence can develop with continued use. The risk increases with higher doses and longer duration. That’s why it’s usually prescribed short-term and closely monitored.

faqs.q: How do I taper off oxazepam safely?
faqs.a: If you’ve been taking it regularly, don’t stop suddenly. A common approach is gradual dose reduction—often around 20-25% per week for lower-risk situations, or ~25% every 1-2 weeks for longer-term or higher-dose use, adjusted to your symptoms and safety factors. Some clinicians consider switching to a longer-acting benzodiazepine in select cases to smooth the taper. The right taper is the one your body tolerates.

faqs.q: Is oxazepam safe for older adults?
faqs.a: Benzodiazepines are generally avoided in adults 65+ because they increase risk of confusion, delirium, falls, fractures, and car accidents. Oxazepam may still be used when there’s a strong reason (like alcohol withdrawal or severe anxiety that isn’t responding to safer options), but dosing should be low, cautious, and time-limited.

faqs.q: Is oxazepam safer if you have liver problems?
faqs.a: Oxazepam is often considered when hepatic concerns exist because it’s metabolized mainly through glucuronidation (a phase II pathway) and doesn’t rely on the same oxidation pathways as some other benzodiazepines. That said, “safer” doesn’t mean “risk-free”—sedation, falls, and interactions can still happen.

faqs.q: Does oxazepam treat depression or psychosis?
faqs.a: No. Oxazepam is not an antidepressant and not an antipsychotic. It can reduce anxiety symptoms, but it does not treat the core biology of depression, and it is not indicated for psychosis.

faqs.q: What are the most common oxazepam side effects?
faqs.a: The big ones are sleepiness, dizziness, brain fog/slowed thinking, and unsteady coordination. Memory issues can also happen. If you notice severe sedation, slurred speech, or wobbliness, your dose may be too high—or you may be combining it with something else sedating.

faqs.q: Can oxazepam be used in pregnancy or breastfeeding?
faqs.a: Sometimes, but it requires careful risk-benefit discussion. Benzodiazepines can affect the newborn (sedation or withdrawal symptoms), especially with late-pregnancy exposure. For alcohol withdrawal during pregnancy, benzodiazepines are commonly used and inpatient monitoring is often recommended. During breastfeeding, oxazepam can be present in milk, so if it’s used, the lowest effective dose and infant monitoring for sedation/feeding issues are important.
